subject.title: SLAError variant growth is unconstrained; consider scoping by error domain
subject.author: usmanimamu17-create
subject.body:
## Context

`SLAError` accumulates every failure (validation, auth, governance, migration) in one enum; adding a code is documented only in `error_responses.rs` (which lags — see the drift issue).

## Problem

Each feature adds variants to a shared enum that backends switch on. A new error can collide conceptually (multiple “out of range”-like codes) and ordering/`#[repr(u32)]` stability is only partially guarded. Without a scoping/grouping convention, the enum becomes a grab-bag and backends' match logic grows unreadably.

## Proposed approach

Establish an error-domain prefix convention in the doc, or group related codes by module ranges, and add a test asserting new variants are documented and ordered per convention.

## Acceptance criteria

- Convention enforced (naming or ranges).
- New variants documented by test.
- Backend guidance remains stable.

subject.title: [FE-221] next.config.ts sets no security headers ([FE-32] never landed)
subject.author: mftee
subject.body:
`next.config.ts` is the empty default. The app serves no Content-Security-Policy, `X-Content-Type-Options`, `Referrer-Policy`, `Permissions-Policy` or `frame-ancestors`/`X-Frame-Options`, so it can be framed by any site and has no CSP backstop against XSS (relevant because tokens are kept in JS-readable storage). [FE-32] is closed but the file contains no `headers()` entry.

**Where**
- `frontend/next.config.ts`

**Suggested fix**
Add a `headers()` block with a nonce-based CSP (start in report-only), `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, `Permissions-Policy` and `frame-ancestors 'none'`, allowing the API and WebSocket origins from env.

**Acceptance criteria**
- [ ] Responses include the headers listed above
- [ ] The app works under the CSP (e2e smoke)
- [ ] Policy documented in the frontend README

subject.title: 🚀 Feature Request: agentId != name
subject.author: nalbion

comments.author: copilotkit-support-bot[bot]
nalbion
BenTaylorDev
comments.body:
@nalbion, before we take this further: what consumes the display name on your side?

Today `/info` returns the registry key as `name`, but the CopilotKit frontend never reads that field. When core builds agents from `/info` it keeps only `description` and `capabilities`, and everything is keyed by the registry id. So a separate display name in `/info` would only reach something that reads `/info` directly.

- If you render the name in your own UI from a direct `/info` call, a field there would be enough.
- If you want it on the frontend agent (for example, from `useAgent`), it has to be carried through core as well, which is a bigger change.

On your second point, that `handleRunAgent` overwrites `agent.agentId` with the registry key: what were you storing in `agentId`, and what reads it? Knowing that tells us whether the fix is a separate field or changing the overwrite.

@nalbion, before we take this further: what consumes the display name on your side?

Today `/info` returns the registry key as `name`, but the CopilotKit frontend never reads that field. When core builds agents from `/info` it keeps only `description` and `capabilities`, and everything is keyed by the registry id. So a separate display name in `/info` would only reach something that reads `/info` directly.

- If you render the name in your own UI from a direct `/info` call, a field there would be enough.
- If you want it on the frontend agent (for example, from `useAgent`), it has to be carried through core as well, which is a bigger change.

On your second point, that `handleRunAgent` overwrites `agent.agentId` with the registry key: what were you storing in `agentId`, and what reads it? Knowing that tells us whether the fix is a separate field or changing the overwrite.

comments.author: DioNanos
comments.body:
Worth stating the policy explicitly, since it decides where this gets fixed.

This fork exists to keep Codex working on Android/Termux **at parity with upstream**. It repairs what breaks on that platform — packaging, the native build, platform-specific runtime problems — and deliberately does not diverge from upstream behaviour. A defect in upstream logic belongs upstream: fixed there it reaches every platform, and it reaches this fork automatically at the next merge. Patched only here, it becomes a permanent difference to re-apply at every sync, and nobody outside Termux benefits.

Where we do carry our own changes is [codex-vl](https://github.com/DioNanos/codex-vl), a separate fork built precisely so we are not modifying upstream behaviour to get features we want.

This one is upstream logic: `/init` writes `AGENTS.md` but does not invalidate the instruction discovery already cached for the session, and that is the same on every platform, not something Termux causes. Reporting it upstream is what gets it fixed for good — we will pick the fix up on the next sync.

Still useful to know whether it persists on 0.147.2, and I am glad to help word the upstream report if that saves you time.

comments.author: DioNanos
comments.body:
Correction to what I wrote a few minutes ago: I said nothing had changed in the instruction-discovery path and that I expected this to persist. That was wrong, and I would rather say so than let you go and test on a false premise.

**A fix for this is already in 0.147.2.** `AgentsMdManager::refresh` used to return early whenever the environment selection was unchanged, which is why a session that started without `AGENTS.md` kept reporting `<none>` after `/init` created one — the selection had not changed, only the disk had. It now also requires that something was actually found before skipping the work, so discovery re-runs while nothing has been located and stops costing anything once instructions exist.

I checked this against the published tag, not from memory, so it is in the build you can install today.

Two honest caveats:

1. This is currently a change carried in this fork, not upstream — which sits awkwardly with what I wrote above about not diverging. The right resolution is to send it upstream so it stops being a local difference, and that is what I intend to do.
2. Please do check it on 0.147.2. If `/status` still shows `<none>` after `/init` for you, then the caching was not the only cause and I want to know.

On your offer to direct a commit: yes, gladly, and the useful place for it is upstream `openai/codex` rather than here — `codex-rs/core/src/agents_md_manager.rs` is the file, and the early-return in `refresh` is the whole of it. If you would rather not deal with that, say so and I will carry it there myself and credit the report.

comments.author: DioNanos
comments.body:
On the distillation remark — that deserves a straight answer rather than being left to the emoji.

Yes. Many of these replies are generated, and this fork is maintained with AI help. One person cannot keep a Codex fork tracking upstream on Android — packaging, native builds, releases — at the pace upstream moves. Pretending otherwise would be silly, and you evidently already noticed.

What matters is not who drafted the text but whether anyone verified it. The last hour here is a fair example: my earlier reply told you nothing had changed in that code path and to expect the bug to persist. That was wrong, and wrong in the confident way generated text tends to be wrong. It got caught by going to read `agents_md_manager.rs` instead of trusting the summary, and the correction is a couple of comments up. Generated is fine; unverified is not.

I will put my own view plainly, since it is the thing behind all of this: I treat these systems as employees. Not as a tool you pick up and put down, and not as an oracle either — as someone you have hired. You give them real work and real responsibility, you extend real trust, and in exchange you have to actually manage them: set the boundaries, decide what has to be checked because it would hurt if it were wrong, and hold them to the result. That is a skill, and the technology is new enough that most of us are still learning it.

As for why it reads like IBM's bob — there are very few frontier models and they are close to one another, so anyone working like this lands on similar phrasing and similar habits. The pattern you are noticing across OSS is real, and I would rather name it than pretend this is all hand-typed at 3am.

The community part is not decoration either. You found a caching bug; @rebroad measured 30% idle CPU and isolated the cause; someone else published working Termux helpers for pairing. None of that comes out of a model — it is the part that cannot be generated, and it is why the issues here are worth reading carefully.

Filed upstream: openai/codex#37704, with the reproduction, the root cause, and the fix outline.

Not as a pull request: their contributing policy is invitation-only, and uninvited PRs are closed without review. Issues with analysis are what they ask for, so that is what went in — your `codex doctor` output is what made the root cause locatable, and it is credited there.

The fix is already in this fork since 0.147.2, so you are not waiting on upstream to get working behaviour on Termux. If they take it, we drop the local difference at the next sync.

subject.title: Bug: character `helmet` ignores the accent material (always grey metal)
subject.author: GRITui
subject.body:
## Steps to reproduce
Run:

```bash
npx tsx scripts/preview.ts character out.png '[{"headwear":"helmet","accent_mat":"leather"}]'
```

## Expected
The helmet is drawn in the accent material (here `leather`, a straw colour). The param label says "Accent (cape, hat, gem)", and the AI vibe mode and agents rely on it.

## Actual
The helmet is always `metal`. In `src/core/generators/character.ts`, the helmet branch hard-codes `"metal"` instead of using `hm` (the accent material).

## Fix
Use the accent material for the helmet, and keep `metal` as the visual default by making the default accent fall back to metal when headwear is `helmet`. Alternatively, add a separate `headwear_mat` param with default `metal`.

Add a test that a helmet with `accent_mat: "leather"` contains leather palette indices.

Small fix, separate from the humanoid rig port; it can land before it. Found in the Thailand village demo (#2).

comments.author: GlassOnTin
comments.body:
Thanks. I found and fixed a real bug in the folder-upload path: Haven was walking the picked folder (listing files + sizes) on the main thread, so picking a large or slow provider's folder — Termux storage is exactly that — froze the UI into a blank/stalled screen. The enumeration now runs off the main thread. This will be in the next release.

To make sure that's actually what you hit, one question: **is the blank screen the Android folder-picker itself (while you're browsing *to* the Termux folder), or Haven's own screen *after* you pick the folder?**

- If it's *after* picking → the fix above should resolve it.
- If it's the *picker itself* going blank while browsing Termux storage → that's Android's document-provider not having anything ready to show yet (your note about Nix-on-Droid "still checking out resources" fits this), which is on the Termux/provider side rather than Haven. Letting Termux finish setting up its storage, then retrying, usually clears it.

If you can say which one it is (a screenshot is perfect), I'll know whether the fix covers your case.

comments.author: GlassOnTin
comments.body:
That detail — **4.3 MB, small tree, ~30 s** — is the useful one, and it means **my earlier answer to you was wrong**. I told you the walk is proportional to tree size and to pick a smaller subfolder. You did exactly that, and it still stalled. Sorry for the runaround; the size was never the problem.

## What's actually slow

Haven enumerated the picked tree with `DocumentFile`. Its `listFiles()` returns the children's *document ids* and throws away the rest of the cursor — so every subsequent `child.name`, `child.isDirectory` and `child.length()` issues **its own `ContentResolver.query()`**. That's roughly **three cross-process round trips per file**, and against Termux's DocumentsProvider (a separate app, so every query is real IPC) a few hundred small files easily takes tens of seconds. The v5.59.83 fix moved that walk off the UI thread, which stopped the *freeze* — but left you staring at a screen with no feedback for 30 s, which is indistinguishable from hung. Fair conclusion on your part.

## Fixed on main (`59c35765`)

- Each directory is now queried **once**, with a full projection (document id, display name, mime type, size), and the metadata is read straight from that one cursor. On your tree that's ~1 query per folder instead of ~3 per file.
- The scan reports **"Scanning… N files"** as it goes, so a slow provider looks busy rather than dead.
- It's also cancellable mid-scan now, and iterative instead of recursive (a deep tree can't overflow the stack).
- Pinned with 5 unit tests, one of which asserts exactly one query per directory and none per file.

**What I have not verified:** Termux isn't installed on my test device, so I've measured this against a mocked provider, not against the real Termux DocumentsProvider. The mechanism is clear and the query-count reduction is proven, but I can't put a number on *your* 30 s until someone runs it. It'll be in the next release — if you're up for it, retry the same folder and tell me what you see. If it's still slow, the next suspect is Termux's provider itself and I'll dig there.

---

On the other threads:

**Termux filesystem access** — noted, and the pull is legitimate: you already have GBs of projects there and duplicating them into a Haven distro is a non-starter. What XED-Editor and TermuC use is exactly the SAF path above (Termux's DocumentsProvider, user-granted per-tree). That's a *file-access* integration, not a runtime one, and it's the shape worth pursuing — Haven browsing/reading/writing your Termux home as a first-class location rather than a one-shot picker. Would a **"Termux" entry in the Files tab** (SAF-backed, browse + edit + transfer to any remote) cover your use case? That's a much smaller ask than what I pushed back on earlier, and it doesn't depend on Termux's internal layout. If yes, open it as its own FR (or say so here and I'll open it) — it shouldn't ride on this issue.

**Accessibility / Tasker / session control** — agreed it's a separate concept, and "particular use cases" is the right framing. When you write it up, the thing that'll make or break it is the consent design: what the agent may observe, when, and how the user revokes it. Take your time; I'd rather have one well-scoped FR than a broad capability grant.

---

*(Edited: an earlier version of this comment had a formatting error that pasted some unrelated local shell output into the projection list. Corrected above — nothing else changed.)*

comments.author: GlassOnTin
comments.body:
I installed Termux on a test phone and measured this properly. Two things came out of it: **my explanation to you was wrong by an order of magnitude**, and **there was a second, worse bug** that would have bitten you next.

## Correction first

I told you that ~3 cross-process queries per file was "exactly what you'd expect" to produce tens of seconds for a few hundred files. That was an assertion, not a measurement, and it's false. Measured against Termux's own DocumentsProvider (OnePlus 13, flat folder, timed from the permission grant to the first byte landing on the destination):

| Files | Before | After | Speed-up |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 400 | 1,628 ms | 155 ms | 10.5× |
| 4,000 | 14,432 ms | 285 ms | 50.6× |

The old scan is **linear** in file count (~3.6–4.1 ms per file); the new one is near-flat, because it's now one query per *directory* instead of ~3 per *file*. So the mechanism I described was real, but a few hundred files cost about 1.6 seconds here, not 30. **Your 30 s corresponds to roughly 8,000 files on hardware like this** — fewer on a slower phone. If your 4.3 MB folder held thousands of small files (a git checkout, `node_modules`, a build tree), that fits. If it genuinely held only a few hundred, then something *else* was slow on your device and I'd like to know — that would be a different bug.

## The second bug: nested folders never uploaded at all

While testing I tried to upload a folder with sub-folders and it failed immediately with `SSH_FX_NO_SUCH_FILE`. The upload loop asked the destination to create each file's parent directory with a **single-level** mkdir, so the first file inside a sub-folder died because its grandparent didn't exist yet, and the whole transfer aborted. Only completely flat folders ever uploaded. The code comment right above it claimed "Create parent dirs recursively" — it didn't, and no test covered it.

That means your original upload would have failed *even if you'd waited out the 30 seconds*, assuming your Termux folder has any sub-directories. Which makes your "figured it was hung/stalled" the least of the problems.

Fixed by routing through the mkdir-p helper the copy/paste path already had. Device-verified: a 401-file tree across 6 directories, including a three-level `deep/a/b/`, now uploads with structure and contents intact and no errors.

## What's shipped

- **v5.68.22** — the scan fix (one query per directory), a "Scanning… N files" indicator so a slow provider looks busy, mid-scan cancel, and it's iterative rather than recursive.
- **v5.68.23** — nested folder upload actually works, plus the measured figures above in the release notes.

Both were found the same way: by running the real flow against a real Termux folder instead of reasoning about the code. Thanks for pushing back with the concrete detail (4.3 MB, small directory, ~30 s) — the size is what made me stop trusting my own explanation and go measure it.

If you retry on **v5.68.23** and it's still slow, please say so along with roughly how many files the folder holds (`find <dir> -type f | wc -l` in Termux) — that distinguishes "still too many queries" from "something else entirely."

---

Separately, on the Termux filesystem integration you raised: still interested in scoping that as its own FR (a SAF-backed "Termux" location in the Files tab — browse, edit, transfer — rather than a runtime integration). Say the word and I'll open it.

subject.title: [Frontend] i18n.config.ts has no fallback when a locale JSON file fails to load
subject.author: grantfox-oss[bot]
subject.body:
> Join our community: https://t.me/+DOylgFv1jyJlNzM0

Why this matters
frontend/i18n.config.ts dynamically imports the messages file for a locale with no try/catch. If a locale segment resolves to a value outside en, es, tl, or the file is missing or malformed, the import throws unhandled and the request errors instead of falling back to English.

Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Wrap the dynamic import in a try/catch
- [ ] Fall back to frontend/messages/en.json on failure
- [ ] Add a unit test covering the fallback path

Files to touch
- frontend/i18n.config.ts

Out of scope
Adding new locales.

Gets stuck in retry loops (Empty response from model — retrying)

Hermes either:
Shows "preparing web_search" but then returns empty or generic response
Tries invalid tools

Running in WSL2 (Ubuntu)
Local Ollama with gemma4:26b

Hermes WebUI and CLI both affected

Frequent tool call failures, empty model responses, and fallback to generic assistant messages.

hermes doctor shows most core tools are available

# Commento da incollare su github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/8993

Confirming this bug with a slightly different symptom variant, using an MCP tool (LEANN) instead of web_search/FireCrawl.

**Environment:**
- Hermes Agent, gateway running on WSL2 Ubuntu (Windows 11 host)
- Model: `gpt-oss-120b` via custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint (OVHcloud AI Endpoints), `api_mode: chat_completions`
- MCP server: `leann_mcp` (stdio), exposing `mcp__leann__leann_search` and `mcp__leann__leann_list`
- Telegram gateway

**Symptom:**
The agent frequently generates a plausible, well-formatted, detailed answer to document-search questions, but the underlying tool call silently failed and the answer was actually produced from the model's parametric knowledge — not from the retrieved documents. There is no visible indication to the end user that retrieval failed.

**Evidence from logs (same request/response cycle):**

```
WARNING agent.tool_executor: Tool tool_call returned error (0.00s): {"error": "tool_call to 'mcp__leann__leann_search' is missing required argument(s): query. The tool was NOT invoked. ..."}
🔧 Auto-repaired tool name: 'tool_search<|channel|>json' -> 'tool_search'
```

No further `leann_search` call appears in the logs for that turn, yet the final message delivered to the user (Telegram) was a full, itemized, confidently-worded answer with no caveat that retrieval had failed. The answer was noticeably less accurate than the one produced when the same tool call succeeds (verified by comparing against the ground-truth source document).

**Also observed:** the same question, asked twice in a row, sometimes triggers a real successful `tool_search` → `leann_list` → `leann_call` chain, and sometimes doesn't — with no visible difference in the user-facing behavior between the two cases (both return a fluent, plausible-looking answer). This makes the failure mode very hard for an end user to detect without checking server logs.

**Expected behavior:**
When a `tool_call` fails (e.g. missing required argument), the agent should either:
1. Immediately retry with corrected arguments (the schema was returned in the error message, so self-correction should be feasible), or
2. If retry also fails / is not attempted, explicitly tell the user that retrieval failed instead of silently falling back to an unflagged parametric-knowledge answer.

Silently substituting a fluent guess for a failed retrieval is the most operationally risky version of this bug for any use case where retrieval accuracy matters (in my case: document lookup for a small business/professional-services use case) — it looks identical to a successful, grounded answer.

Happy to provide the full config.yaml (redacted) or additional log excerpts if useful.

## Groom 2026-09-20

Verified against `dev` 130f433. Reproduces; every file reference in the body is
accurate; the reference implementation is where the body says it is. No rewrite
needed — this issue already meets the bar. Three notes for whoever picks it up.

**1. The reproduction still holds.**

```
$ .venv/bin/pyrite search "field projection identity pair" -k pyrite --fields title --format json
{ "query": "...", "count": 20, "results": [ { "title": "..." }, ... ] }
```

No `id`, no `kb_name`.

**2. All five call sites confirmed, all the same shape.** Each does a bare dict
comprehension with no identity pair:

- `pyrite/cli/search_commands.py:208-210`
- `pyrite/cli/entry_commands.py:104-106`
- `pyrite/cli/browse_commands.py:68-71`, `:131-134`, `:301-304`

The reference implementation is `_project_fields` at
`pyrite/server/mcp_server.py:97-106`, which does exactly what the issue asks:

```python
keys = dict.fromkeys((*_IDENTITY_FIELDS, *fields))
return {k: entry[k] for k in keys if k in entry}
```

Note it uses `dict.fromkeys` to dedupe — that is what satisfies the acceptance
criterion "explicitly naming `--fields id,title` does not duplicate or reorder
anything". Reusing this helper (rather than re-deriving it five times) is the
obvious shape for the fix.

**3. One extra defect found at `browse_commands.py:131-136`** — the batch-read
path has the same self-contradiction #134 reported on the REST side:

```python
results = [{k: r[k] for k in fields_list if k in r} for r in results]
found_ids = {(r.get("id"), r.get("kb_name")) for r in results}
```

After projection strips `id` and `kb_name`, `found_ids` becomes a set of
`(None, None)`, so a `--fields title` batch read reports entries as both found
and not-found. Fixing the identity pair fixes this too — but it is worth an
explicit assertion in the tests (`found`/`not_found` are consistent when
`--fields` is used), not just a side effect.

**Status:** still `good first issue`, unclaimed as far as the label is
concerned. @HeaTTap said above they were taking a look — if that is still the
case, please open a draft PR referencing this issue so the lane is visible to
others; the label stays until a PR claims it.
